rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: Rabies risk management guidance covers exposure assessment, post-exposure treatment and public-health management of suspected human cases.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: Prompt treatment after a potential rabies exposure is the most effective way to prevent disease.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: Post-exposure treatment uses rabies vaccine with or without human rabies immunoglobulin according to the assessed exposure risk.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: Risk assessment should combine the country and animal risk with the category of exposure.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: Health professionals should use the current rabies country-risk list rather than relying on an older embedded list.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: People bitten or scratched by a bat in the UK should seek prompt medical assessment because UK bats can carry European bat lyssaviruses.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: People returning to the UK after an overseas exposure should seek medical review even when treatment was started abroad or the exposure occurred weeks earlier.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: The UKHSA rabies post-exposure risk-assessment form was updated on 23 July 2026 and includes current vaccine-alert information.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: Rabies risk depends on country, animal species, exposure route, wound characteristics, prior vaccination, product authenticity and treatment delay.

rows.source: UKHSA rabies risk assessment and post-exposure treatment
rows.verified: Rabies evidence is exposure-, animal-, country-, patient-, treatment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Q fever is an infection caused by the bacterium Coxiella burnetii.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: The infection is usually, but not always, acquired through direct contact with farm animals, especially sheep, cattle and goats.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Q fever can cause a pneumonia-like illness in humans.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: The infection can cause illness and abortion in animals.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Most human cases are sporadic and outbreaks are unpredictable.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Outbreaks may disproportionately affect non-immune populations.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Pregnant people, immunosuppressed people and people with heart-valve disease or vascular grafts should avoid contact with pregnant cattle, sheep, goats and cats.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Prevention guidance links farm-worker protection, zoonosis controls and advice for new and expectant mothers.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Q-fever risk depends on animal infection status, birthing materials, aerosol generation, occupation, proximity, immune status and environmental conditions.

rows.source: UKHSA Q fever prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Q-fever evidence is animal-, holding-, activity-, person-, exposure- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
